On that specific point, the math checks out. A 56K modem under real-world conditions achieves roughly 5 kilobytes per second. A 235-megabyte file would take approximately 19 hours to transfer. The math is correct. The excuse is not. He was not trying to download the file. He was using Remotely Anywhere, the very remote desktop software he had installed on these machines himself. When you operate remote desktop software, you are not transferring the source file. You are streaming a compressed visual feed of the host computer's screen. The moment that image began rendering on a monitor in London, even at 4-bit color, drawing slowly line by line to compensate for dial-up speed, it was no longer only on a server in Houston. It was physically illuminated on his screen. This was 2001 to 2002. The print screen key had been standard hardware since the late 1980s. If the image was visible, capturing it required a single keystroke. Hit print screen. Paste into paint. Save as a bitmap.

segments.speaker: Narrator/Analyst
segments.text: At 4-bit color and low resolution, that screenshot would not be 235 megabytes. It would be 50 kilobytes. Small enough to fit on a floppy disk. Small enough to save in under a second. A floppy disk you could have mailed to every journalist on Earth. McKinnon's defense against this basic technical reality? He claims the Java-based remote viewer did not store data locally, and he was disconnected before he could act. But that is not how operating systems function. You do not need the source file to take a screenshot. You only need the pixels rendering on your glass. He described spending minutes examining this image. Enough time to catalog the geodesic spheres, the absence of seams, the absence of riveting. Minutes of detailed visual observation, but not enough time to press one key. Independent researchers who have rigorously audited McKinnon's claims have assigned them corroboration confidence scores. The non-terrestrial officer's spreadsheet? Zero out of five. The NASA cigar-shaped craft image? One out of five. And that single point is awarded only because McKinnon's description has remained consistent enough across interviews to suggest he genuinely believes it. Not because a single piece of independently verifiable evidence exists. No screenshots. No file hashes. No partial metadata. No matching archival records at NASA.

segments.speaker: Narrator/Analyst
segments.text: And critically, nothing recovered from his seized home computer corroborates either claim. The House of Lords Judgment, which is the most detailed primary source describing what was found on his seized devices, documents copy password files and operating system data. It does not mention extraterrestrial spreadsheets. From a legal standpoint, the UFO narrative proved extraordinarily effective. It transformed McKinnon from a man who had crippled naval logistics during a national security crisis into a sympathetic modern-day David fighting a government Goliath. His decade-long battle against extradition became a high-profile political cause. Supporters viewed him not as a cyber-criminal, but as a fragile truth-seeker being crushed by a superpower. His fight ran. Arrest, June 2005. Extradition order, July 2006. Divisional court dismissal, April 2007. House of Lords Peel dismissed, July 2008. Medical representations. Human rights challenges. Further appeals. Then, on October 16, 2012, Home Secretary Theresa May withdrew the extradition order entirely. Not because he was innocent. Not because the UFO claims were validated. But because medical assessments concluded extradition posed such a severe suicide risk, compounded by his Asperger syndrome and depressive illness, that it would be incompatible to his human rights. He won on compassionate grounds. Not evidentiary ones. The UK prosecution? Director of Public Prosecutions, Keir Starmer, stated publicly that a domestic case faced significant practical and evidential obstacles. The time elapsed, the cross-border logistics, the difficulty of assembling charges that would reflect the full extent of the alleged criminality. He was never charged in the UK either. The man who allegedly committed the biggest military breach in US history walked free on both sides of the Atlantic. No verdict, no acquittal, no trial. Just a decade of headlines. And a story that will apparently never be fully resolved. One final footnote. In late 2023, the BBC commissioned a full scripted dramatization of the extradition fight. The People vs. Gary McKinnon. A proper television drama 20 years after the intrusions. The cultural appetite for this story shows no sign of fading. Whether that is because people genuinely believe Gary found something real, or because the story is simply too cinematic not to tell, is perhaps itself the most revealing data point of all.

segments.text: In the end,

segments.speaker: Narrator/Analyst
segments.text: it wasn't about firewalls or passwords. It wasn't about network logs or headlines or wiped hard drives. It was about a mirror. A mirror held up to a world that would much rather believe in a cigar-shaped spaceship than the terrifyingly simple truth. Gary McKinnon didn't discover a secret space. He simply knocked on a poorly secured door. And when that door creaked open, he saw exactly what he wanted to see. They called him a threat, a criminal. But the real threat was the question his story forced us to ask. Who is more dangerous? The man who lies? Or the world that refuses to look at the math? A man who was smoking a lot of dope at the time couldn't remember the names of the ships in humanity's secret space fleet and never once pressed print screen. Maybe silence is safety. But in the digital age, the most dangerous act is believing without proof.
